SDG MPTF Kenya

description.narrative: Insatsen var initialt ett stöd till FN:s nya landprogram för Kenya, Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (SDCF), 2022-2026, som kanaliseras genom en Multi Partner Trust Fund för ändamålet. Det svenska stödet ska främst användas för kapacitetsstärkning av MPTF:s management i Nairobi, inklusive sekretariatet för SDG Partnership Platform, båda inhysta under UN Resident Coordinator's Office (UNRCO). Kapacitetsstärkningen riktar sig främst mot områdena ungdomar och sysselsättning; katastrofriskreduceringe och resiliens; miljö, klimat och grön finansiering samt hanteringen av SDGPP. Ytterligare bidrag har därefter givits till fonden för att stödja särskilda ändamål genom sk Joint Programs.

The contribution was initially a support to the UN:s new country program for Kenya - the Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework (SDCF), 2022-2026, which is channeled through the Multi Partner Trust Fund set up for this purpose. The Swedish support will primarily be used for capacity strengthening of the MPTF's management in Nairobi, including the Secretariat for the SDG Partnership Platform, both hosted within the UN Resident Coordinator's Office (UNRCO). The capacity strengthening is focused on the areas of youth and employment; disaster risk reduction and resilience; environment, climate and green financing; and SDGPP management. Additional contributions to the Fund have thereafter been provided for special purposes through so called Joint Programs.

The main objectives of the intervention are:
- improved coordination of the UNCT, together with GoK, donors and other stakeholders, for a more effective and efficient implementation of the UNSDCF in alignment with Kenya's development plans;
- contribute to enhanced resource mobilization through the SDGPP and development of innovative finance solutions for investments in prioritised sectors (and sub-sectors) as identfied by Kenya and in the SDCF.
The SDG MPTF Kenya was established in July 2022, with the purpose to support the delivery of UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework 2022 2026, enhance the UN to deliver as one through Joint Programs and to support the country in achieving the SDGs. The Fund builds on the existing Partnerships Platform (SDGPP) that was established in 2017 to support the UNDAF 20182022. Sida's first contribution is loosely earmarked to the Fund's "Enabler Window", and more specifically for Strengthening the Capacity of the SDG MPTF Kenya Secretariat (the Secretariat) by financing four positions at the RCO and SDGPP, as well as a smaller budget for "emerging, strategic issues". A second contribution to the Fund was agreed upon in a first amendment to the MPTF SAA and disbursed in late December 2022, earmarked for a Joint Program on drought response and resilience under the Window for Strategic Pillar 2, "Planet and Prosperity". A third contribution to the Fund was agreed upon in a second amendment to the MPTF SAA and disbursed in late December 2023, earmarked for a bridge Joint Program on Social and Child Protection under the Window for Strategic Pillar 1, "People and Peace". The objectives of the intervention have, thus, been updated with regards to the additional funding to the MPTF by these amendments.
The main objectives of the intervention are: - improved coordination of the UNCT, together with GoK, donors and other stakeholders, for a more effective and efficient implementation of the UNSDCF in alignment with Kenya's development plans; - contribute to enhanced resource mobilization through the SDGPP and development of innovative finance solutions for investments in prioritized sectors (and sub-sectors) as identified by Kenya and in the SDCF.
For amendment I: The main purpose and overall objective is to enhance response and recovery for communities affected by drought in Northern Kenya while enhancing long term climate resilience response and recovery targeting 75,000 people and 200,000 livestock. The specific objectives are: - to provide improved access to safe water and hygiene for 75,000 drought affected vulnerable people and 200,000 livestock in Turkana, Garissa, Wajir, Mandera, and Marsabit counties by ensuring continued availability and access to essential services and strengthened climate smart food production for 1,000 households impacted by the drought in Garissa, Turkana and Tana River counties.
For amendment II: The expected results are: - To enhance the capacity and opportunities for the poor and vulnerable to improve and sustain their livelihoods and welfare; - To facilitate and follow up successful achievement of government's commitment to expand social protection coverage including cost sharing whenever possible; - Social and child protection systems have enhanced technical and financial capacity to develop and manage programs at scale; - Functional coordination at the national and county levels for inter-sectoral linkages is enhanced; - Government and partners have financial and technical capacity to review, develop and implement policies, legislation and strategies delivering on the right to social protection and child protection-
For amendment III: The expected results for the Joint Program are: - To support coordination, data management and evidence based policymaking, planning and budgeting for enhanced child protection and social protection outcomes - Enhanced systems and capacity of the national and county governments, non-state institutions and communities to efficiently deliver well-coordinated, inclusive, accessible, equitable and resilient/shock-responsive social and child protection services to Kenyans, addressing multiple dimensions of poverty and vulnerability across the life cycle. -Enhanced capacity of national and county governments, non state institutions and communities to strengthen and expand inclusive and sustainable child protection and social protection programmes and systems For this Joint Program Swedish contribution to the MPTF, the interventions objectives are hereby updated with regards to the funding for Social and Child Protection

description.narrative:
The Fund Reports annually in May on Fund Status and Progress as per the previous calendar year. The Annual Report submitted in May 2024, hence, covers the period 1st January to 31st December 2023 and provides a detailed summary of consolidated results and achievements as well as the financial status of the MPTF. During 2023, Sweden's contributions to the MPTF has continued to support the RCO through the Enabler Window, and also funded Joint Programs for Disaster Risk Reduction (as a one off emergency and resilience building drought response) and Social and Child Protection respectively. The latter being a bridging support as the long-term JP is being finalized.
Examples of results and achievements reported include: Under the Enabler Window, the Secretariat: - Contributed to enhanced Coordination, efficient management, programmatic facilitation for joint action, and crosscutting catalytic support. - Facilitated youth participation in various processes and summits. For example, the representation of young people in all joint programs development processes, in which youth voices were actively included to ensure their perspectives were integrated into the program design. A significant outcome of these efforts was the development of a joint programspecifically focused on the youth centered on youth empowerment through skills development, employment, and civic engagement which is now being implemented. - Provided technical support and coordination to the UN Adolescent and Youth Technical Working Group, which serves as a platform for UN agencies to coordinate joint efforts towards youth empowerment. - Supported UN Kenyas active participation in various high-level multi-stakeholder youth empowerment technical working groups. - Provided technical support towards the ongoing harmonization of government investments in the youth sector. The process involved high level technical alignment involving the Generation Unlimited, GenU (part of a global initiative to equip young people aged between ten (10 years) and twenty four (24 years) with the skills necessary to thrive in the society and the workforce). -Technical support and coordination was provided for the delivery of the YouthConnekt Africa Summit 2023, hosted in Nairobi, a significant event that brings together young people, government officials, corporate leaders, and development champions to empower African youth. The summit aims at enhancing the knowledge, experiences, and skills of African youth while investing in their ideas, innovations, and initiatives, with the overarching goal to harness Africas demographic dividends by 2030. - Provided technical support preceding the Inter-Governmental Authority on Development (IGAD) inter-ministerial meeting held in Kenya in September 2023. The meeting resulted in the adoption of the IGAD Youth Policy, a significant framework aimed at promoting youth rights in the IGAD Region. The IGAD Youth Policy is a crucial tool for guiding and mainstreaming youth priorities in policies, laws, and programmes designed to empower youth and ensure their meaningful participation in political processes. - Provided support to the Resident Coordinator and the UN Country Team (UNCT) on environment and climate initiatives, aligning with Kenya's national ambitions, including strategic Support ahead of and during the Africa Climate Summit (ACS) 2023, held in Nairobi, and participation in advocacy platforms:
* The 2023 ACS served as a central platform for key stakeholders across the continent to come together and address the pressing climate challenges facing Africa. UNCT showcased its joint leadership in climate action and contributed to mobilise support for ambitious climate goals, and advance the continent's sustainable development agenda in the face of climate change. The Joint Programs under co-creation on "Sustainable Production and Consumption in the Green and Blue Economies" and "Sustainable agriculture, land, and water/ocean use" were presented.
- Held a side event addressing climate related social vulnerabilities and the transition to more sustainable food systems in Africa, highlighting various risks affecting sustainability and environmental crime.
- Held a side event focusing on just transition experiences in Africa and strategies to integrate just transition principles into the implementation of national environment and climate policies across the continent.
- Support was also provided for the initiative on Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL) and the launch of GoKs Green Growth and Investment Plan, which outlines pathways for Kenya to develop its energy systems in alignment with its economic ambitions and the goal of achieving net zero carbon emissions. Technical support was provided to the Government of Kenya in the drafting of the Nairobi Declaration, an eleven point call to action proclaiming African States' unified stance on climate action ahead of the 28th United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP28).
* Participation in Advocacy Platforms included: - The Kenya Carbon Markets Conference hosted by the office of the President - The Mobile World Congress (MWC) Africa - The GSM (Global System for Mobile communication) Association (GSMA). - Round table discussions on climate financing, focusing on engaging stakeholders in discussions surrounding carbon finance, particularly in relation to carbon markets and the process of obtaining carbon accreditation. They also aim to to equip startups and other stakeholders with the necessary knowledge and skills to enter the carbon credits space, potentially creating new revenue streams while contributing to climate resilience and adaptation efforts. - Round table discussions on Climate and Humanitarian action: the role of mobile and digital technology in disaster preparedness and response, early warning systems, cash transfers, and carbon markets. - Bilateral and convened sessions, of which one immediate result is the inception of a biodiversity and innovative finance (including carbon markets) joint program. - Assisted the UNCT in seeking alternative financing sources to complement the roll-out of joint programs. - Played a crucial role in developing the Disaster Risk Reduction joint program, which aims to address both the immediate needs of communities affected by disasters and long-term resilience building initiatives. - Coordination efforts of UNCT led by the Secretariat in the disaster response and management sector, contributing to the the development of a National Disaster Risk Management Bill in Kenya, which aims to enhance coordination and coherence in Disaster Risk Management (DRM) efforts, establish institutional structures at various administrative levels (national, county, sub- county, and ward), and improve coordination between national and county governments. Including the disaster risk management cycle and mainstreaming gender and other inclusion issues within the NDRM Bill No.24 of 2023 demonstrates a commitment to comprehensive and inclusive disaster risk management practices. Currently, the bill is awaiting its second reading at the National Assembly. The bill also envisions that counties will develop their DRM Bills to further strengthen disaster risk management capacities at the local level.
- Catalytic Support through the RC's Seed Fund for Emerging Opportunities: * An independent review of Kenyas Peace Building Architecture (PBA) was initiated, with the purpose to evaluate the achievements and obstacles encountered by Kenya's Peacebuilding Architecture, its ability to address emerging challenges such as violent extremism, climate security issues, digital peace building, and the utilization of data for prevention and sustaining peace. It aims to explore sustainable strategies for peace building financing and to provide recommendations to the Government, the UN, and key stakeholders. The review encompasses 33 counties in Kenya and involves expert level consultations at the national level, along with futures workshops to formulate recommendations. Moreover, technical research was facilitated to support the drafting process of the PBA report. * UNCT's collective efforts to deliver as one during the 2023 Africa Climate Summit (ACS) was supported (see above) * Coordination of UNCT's climate initiatives (led by UNDP) and food security resilience initiatives (led by FAO) was facilitated.
- Under the Planet and Prosperity Window: Trough the JP for Response and Resilience Building in Kenya (implemented by UNDP and UNICEF) Sweden contributed to address the impacts of drought in 6 counties, including building long-term resilience through strengthening access to safe and adequate water, water management, and climate smart food production for households. Over this reporting period, the project reached a total of 85,914 direct beneficiaries (41,109 male 44,805 female) and 54,615 people (30725 female and 23625 male) indirect beneficiaries.
- Under the People and Peace Thematic Window: Sweden contributed with one year's funding to the bridging JP for Social and Child Protection (implemented by WFP and UNICEF). Since the disbursement to the MPTF only was made in December 2023, no activities were carried out during this reporting period and results can, hence, not be attributed to this reporting period.
The previous phase of the social and child protection joint programme (including the bridging period supported through the SDG-MPTF) had the overall goal to ensure that people in Kenya, especially the most vulnerable groups, live in dignity, are free from poverty, hunger, violence, abuse and exploitation, to be able to exploit their full human capabilities and contribute to the national development. The programme contributed and enhanced social and child protection in Kenya through three areas:
a) Technical assistance to develop and implement legislation, policies, and strategies on social protection.
b) Systems strengthening, enhanced capacity and increased efficiencies in the delivery of social protection programmes.
c) Strengthen inter-sectoral coordination and linkages at the national and decentralised (county) level.
Based on the three objective areas above, the joint program was assessed successful ofcourse with challenges and gaps as later highlighted. Results were assessed in terms of program relevance, coherence, effectiveness and sustainability as explained below:
Relevance: Was the joint program relevant?
1. The design of the Joint Programme allowed it to be implemented flexibly and respond to the most promising opportunities in the social and child protection sectors. The Theory of Change and Output Areas informing the Joint Programmes design were internally coherent. They led to the implementing partners supporting relevant interventions which have helped to strengthen the social and child protection sectors. Within the output areas, the Joint Programme selected interventions which reflected both GoK priorities and possibilities, as well as global norms and standards. When there was a trade-off to be made, the Joint Programme rightly aligned most closely with the GoK.
2. Policy and Legislation, the Joint Programme supported the most urgent and important issues. At national level, these included the Childrens Act, the Huduma Bill, the Care Reform Strategy, the Social Assistance Act, and the Social Protection Policy review. At county level, this included (but is not limited to) the Mombasa Social Protection Strategy, the Wajir People with Disabilities Act, the Makueni Social Protection Policy, and the West Pokot draft Child Protection Policy.
3. Systems Strengthening and Service Delivery, the Joint Programme supported some, but not all, critical issues. The selection of interventions aligned with the most urgent issues in the sectors. The implementing partners supported highly relevant enhancements for management information systems, including the Enhanced Single Registry (ESR), the Consolidated Cash Transfer Programme Management Information System (CCTP-MIS) and the Child Protection Management Information System (CPMIS). Capacity in the social and child protection workforce was boosted through an innovative partnership with the Kenya School of Government (KSG) that filled a substantial gap in the provision of training opportunities for these sectors in Kenya. Notably, however, the Joint Programme was weaker in supporting better costing, budgeting, and financing for these sectors. This challenge remains as fiscal space for social and child protection is anticipated to remain a seismic bottleneck.
4. Coordination and Inter-sectoral Linkages, the Joint Programme appropriately promoted collaboration within and between the social protection and child protection sectors. This has included through driving initiatives for collaboration between development partners, between development partners and the Government of Kenya (GoK) as well as between county and national levels. . Further, the Joint Programmes focus on strengthening synergies between social protection and child protection was highly relevant to the needs of children (and the GoKs stated objectives).
5. The joint programme worked in counties with comparatively high numbers of people in poverty and where clear opportunities to make progress were perceived. The focus counties showed particularly high levels of relative and absolute monetary and multi-dimensional poverty. However, the selection did exclude some counties that within the implemenation period have had high poverty rates and numbers, such as Mandera and Narok. It is recommended that in the new phase, these counties should be considered for inclusion in future iterations of the programme.
6. The joint programme focused on support to vulnerable groups and households. This aligned closely with the greatest needs of children in Kenya, to global strategies, and to the stated goals of the GoK. Interventions inclined toward groups that are typically hidden, such as children living in street situations or those returning from residential institutional care. The Joint Programme also supported efforts to focus on PLwD (through a National Census) and supported legislation and to service delivery to counties including Wajir through the Wajir People with Disabilities Act) and Mombasa through the Mombasa Social Protection Strategy.
7. The joint programme supported the social protection system in Kenya to become more shock responsive and also adapted its own design to respond to emergent shocks. Shock responsiveness was a very relevant focus, given the countrys climate and ecological vulnerability, as well as low resilience amongst the population owing to high rates of population growth and poverty. The implementing partners supported initiatives which impacted shock responsiveness, notably the development of the Social Registry within the ESR, promoting communities adaptation to shock through reprogramming resources towards the COVID-19 response to support groups experiencing increased vulnerability. The implementing partners also took advantage of opportunities to innovate (such as by piloting the Universal Child Benefit (UCB).
Coherence: Was the joint program coherent?
Broadly, the Joint Programme was coherently operated within the social and child protection landscapes in Kenya. The program leveraged pre-existing relationships and reputations to work closely with the GoK, and other stakeholders, across all output areas. The programmes design facilitated this coherence. It largely took a with the grain approach, providing gap-filling resources to push forward agendas and efforts already in motion (for example, upgrading the ESR), as well as supplement these with new complementary interventions (for example, supporting the STRIDE programme in Mombasa). Taking this approach allowed the Joint Programme to achieve sustainable change (such as policy enactment) and catalyse the impact of investments by other stakeholders. The efforts brought about positive externalities in the form of synergies between other stakeholders in the sector. For example, the GoK reported being able to build new relationships, with other stakeholders, owing to the Joint Programmes interventions.
Effectiveness: Was the joint program effective
The joint programme realized many of its objectives and supported the strengthening of the social and child protection sectors in Kenya.
1. Policy and Legislation. Key legislative results from the program included the enactment of the National Social Protection Act 2024, the passage of national child protection legislation, including the Childrens Bill and the Care Reform Strategy. These pieces of legislation formed and continue to form the backbone of alternative care reform.
2. Systems Strengthening and service delivery, the Joint Programme was most effective in this area. Success was particularly notable in activities enhancing management information systems for social protection and child protection. The development (including partial data collection) of the Social Registry and the upgrades to the ESR and CCTP-MIS improved efficiency, targeting, case management and shock responsiveness of the social protection system. The development of a training programme and curriculum at the KSG was an impressive milestone that expanded the knowledge of social and child protection practitioners across Kenya. The programme was also effective in promoting alternative care reform and designing a national M&E framework for social protection.
3. Coordination and Inter-sectoral Linkages, the Joint Programme realized many of the objectives set out in the design proposal. This included through leadership of UNDAF and the development of coordination mechanisms in these sectors . The program also attempted to stimulate inter-sectoral linkages and integration by promoting Cash Plus programmes and the UCB pilot.
Generally the effectiveness of the Joint Programme was supported by a number of factors. This includes strong engagement, and the utilization of pre-existing relationships, between the implementing partners and the GoK (at all levels). The Joint Programme prioritized GoK leadership, aligning their interventions to pre-existing workplans and strategies. Further, the flexibility of the design and funding of the Joint Programme allowed it to pivot towards emergent opportunities (such as the UCB pilot or the Social Assistance Repeal Bill) and respond to risks and shocks as they arose.
Sustainability: Will the benefit and effect of the joint program last?
1. Elements of the Joint Programme are likely to have impact far beyond its conclusion. The sustainability of the Joint Programmes results were enhanced by a number of factors. First, the focus on enactment of social and child protection policies (at national and county level). Policies and legislation, such as the Childrens Act or the Baringo Social Protection Policy create incentive and accountability structures. Stakeholders in many occassions expressed great anticipation in relation to the long-term impact of these policies, seeing them as underpinning future progress in these sectors.
3. Joint Programme interventions such as the ESR and the National M&E Framework for Social Protection (to mention a few) enhanced supportive structures to drive continued action in these sectors. The different informatiuon systems developed for instance got a strong buy-in from stakeholders, thus increasing their likely maintenance.
4. The program invested in local training and skills development. Not only did this tackle a substantial gap in the capacity of workers in the social and child protection systems (making it a relevant intervention) it also ensured that the right people, with the right skills and attitudes were invoved in pushing forward the program's objectives. The training curriculum developed in collaboration with KSG is particularly notable, as it has facilitated an affordable national programme open for practitioners which and allowed a greater number of practitioners to benefit from it.
